title: Minié rifles and French cliffs won the Alma, not generals' orders
dek: The Franco-British alliance won the Alma through the Highland regiment's Minié rifles and a French flank assault up the cliffs, not through Raglan or Saint-Arnaud's battlefield decisions—Raglan was trapped on an isolated hilltop throughout and could give no orders.
why: This is the prelude to the Light Brigade charge—no charge itself, but it lays out all the personal rifts that made the charge inevitable: Lucan and Cardigan's in-law feud, Captain Nolan's fury. The information density concentrates in the second half and rewards a full listen.
who: Readers interested in British military history, the Crimean War, or organizational decision-making failures, especially those wanting to understand the Light Brigade charge tragedy's deeper roots.
skip: The opening ads (Revolut, Sainsbury's) and podcast cross-promotion at the end can be skipped.

points.h: The allied army did almost no reconnaissance or logistics preparation before attacking Crimea
points.body: The allies' only goal was destroying the Russian Black Sea Fleet at Sevastopol and leaving, but before departure they had no intelligence on Russian troop numbers, Crimean geography, fortress artillery, or even weather. They read a few travel memoirs, decided Crimean winters were mild, brought only summer tents with no winter kit, and gambled they could take it in a week.

points.h: Raglan's hat-box joke about locking the Light Brigade became the whole conflict's setup
points.body: Raglan feared horses and riders would suffer severe disease losses, so he forbade the Light Brigade from reconnaissance patrols. He joked about putting them "in a hat box." This throwaway line became catastrophic: Cardigan wanted battle, the cavalry had nothing to do, resentment accumulated daily, and it planted the emotional powder keg that would explode in the Light Brigade charge days later.

points.h: The cavalry suffered a shameful retreat but blamed the wrong man
points.body: At the Bulganak River, the Light Brigade was formed up to charge Cossack cavalry when Raglan ordered retreat. It was actually the right call—from his high position, Raglan saw Russian infantry and artillery in ambush behind them. But the cavalry couldn't see this. They only felt humiliated in front of Russian and British troops, so they vented all their rage at Lucan, and the mocking nickname "Lord Look-on" was born and spread through the army.

points.h: The Alma was a competition in which general could make the more fatal error
points.body: Historian Cecil Woodham-Smith writes that the battle was won by the ferocity of British soldiers, not their generals—both commanders' incompetence reached the "Crimean War-specific madness" that characterized the conflict. Raglan had no real battle plan, just vague orders to advance. Menshikov miscalculated that the seaside cliffs were unclimbable, and these two fatal miscalculations together determined the outcome.

points.h: French soldiers hand-climbed a cliff and broke the Russian left wing
points.body: Russian commander Menshikov assumed the coastal cliff was impassable, so left it weakly defended. Algerian troops led by Pierre Bosquet—expert climbers—scaled the cliff anyway, fixed ropes to haul up large French numbers, and drove directly into the Russian left. This is what sent Russian officers' wives fleeing in panic from their riverside picnic and broke the entire battle.

points.h: The Minié rifle's first battle—firepower equivalent to half a dozen machine guns
points.body: The Highland regiment, commanded by Colin Campbell (a man who rose by merit rather than buying his commission), used the Minié rifle in combat for the first time. Its range, accuracy, and penetration far exceeded the Russian smoothbore musket. Historian Orlando Figes describes the volley fire as "equivalent to half a dozen machine guns"—this is what let British forces outnumber the enemy, uphill, into the teeth of superior Russian numbers.

points.h: A week of hesitation after victory let Sevastopol escape
points.body: After the Alma, Sevastopol was nearly undefended—only 5,000 Russian troops, and the landward walls were crumbling. Menshikov himself thought it indefensible and ordered withdrawal. But the allies didn't press their advantage. They lingered on the battlefield tending to casualties, and by the time they moved, Russian crews had repaired the defenses day and night and sunk seven ships to block the harbor. What should have been a few days of assault became one of history's longest sieges.

points.h: 25,000 Russian troops massed—the Balaclava battle is about to break
points.body: By October 24, Russians had assembled 25,000 troops, infantry and cavalry plus 78 guns, just outside the Causeway Heights. The goal was simple: seize Balaclava's port and cut the allies' supply line, collapsing the Sevastopol siege without direct assault. When Russian artillery opened up on the redoubts before dawn, Cardigan was still asleep on his yacht—the Battle of Balaclava had begun.
